messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Prosecutor
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ethan sat in the passenger seat of his wife’s car, the late autumn sun low and golden through the windshield, and felt the exhaustion wash over him like a tide he could no longer outrun. He was thirty-three years old, a prosecutor in a mid-sized city, married for six years, and for the past eighteen months he had been living with something he could not name. He had come to his first appointment because his wife, Rachel, had finally said she could not watch him disappear anymore. He had not argued. He was too tired.

The event that had shattered him had taken place on a weekday afternoon in October, two years ago. Ethan had been walking through the central plaza of the county courthouse complex, a public space he crossed every day, when a vehicle-mounted improvised explosive device detonated less than a hundred yards from where he stood. The blast threw him to the ground. He had no memory of the sound itself—only a pressure that seemed to come from inside his skull, and then the ringing, and the smoke, and the bodies. He had scrambled to his feet and moved toward the wreckage. He had pulled at debris. He had tried to help. But the man whose leg he had held while waiting for paramedics had died before they arrived. The woman who had been thrown against a concrete planter had been unconscious and bleeding from her ears. Ethan had stayed until the scene was cleared. He had gone home that night and told Rachel he was fine. He had not been fine.

What troubled him most, he said, was that he could not tell a clear story of what had happened, even to himself. The memory existed not as a narrative but as a series of sensory fragments that arrived without warning and without context. He would be standing in the shower, and suddenly he would be there again—the heat of the blast wave, the grit of pulverized glass on his tongue, the smell of alcohol from a broken bottle of hand sanitizer that had been on a security guard’s desk. That smell, specifically, had become a trigger. He could not walk past a bar without his chest tightening. He could not sit next to someone who had been drinking without feeling his pulse spike. He had stopped going to dinner with colleagues. He had stopped going anywhere.

The memories, when they came, were more real than normal. They had a vividness that ordinary recollections lacked, a kind of brutal clarity that made the present moment feel thin and false. He would be at his desk reviewing case files, and the memory of the blast would descend on him with such force that he would lose track of where he was. The past felt present. It was not remembering; it was reliving. And the worst part, the part that kept him awake at night, was the guilt. He could not forgive himself for not doing more. He had been a prosecutor. His job was to protect people. He should have seen the vulnerability of that plaza. He should have done something. He had failed.

This belief had grown roots. He had come to distrust others in a way he had not before. People smiled, they shook his hand, they said they understood, but he was certain that beneath the surface they were not what they seemed. He had stopped trusting his own judgment. He had stopped trusting anyone’s. At work, he had become withdrawn, delegating trials he would once have fought to lead. His supervisor had noticed. Rachel had noticed. He had noticed himself shrinking.

What finally brought him to seek help was not the nightmares, though they came most nights. It was not the way he flinched at the sound of a car backfiring or a door slamming, though he did. It was the exhaustion. The feeling of being tired all the time, bone-deep tired, as if he had been running for two years without stopping. He had come to believe that he would never feel safe again, and he was not sure he deserved to. But he was also afraid—afraid that if he let himself really think about what happened, he would not be able to put himself back together. He did not know if he wanted to be forgiven. He only knew he could not keep living this way.
